summary.text: The law of total probability is a basic rule that links the overall chance of an outcome to its chances under several separate events.
In one example two factories supply bulbs: X makes 60% and Y makes 40%, and their bulbs last over 5000 hours in 99% and 95% of cases.
Putting these together gives every purchased bulb a 97.4% chance of working for more than 5000 hours.

items.prompt: Factory X's bulbs last over 5000 hours 99% of the time, and factory Y's do so 95% of the time. You buy a bulb without knowing who made it. Roughly where does its chance of lasting fall?

options.label: Below 95%, because mixing makers adds extra risk
Over 99%, because having two makers adds safety
Between 95% and 99%, since it came from one of the two
Exactly 97%, since the two rates are shared evenly

items.explain: The bulb comes from X or from Y, so its overall chance sits between the two factory rates; the example gives 97.4%.

items.prompt: To work out the overall chance that a purchased bulb lasts, which two pieces of information do you need about the factories?

options.label: Each factory's share of the bulbs and each factory's own chance of a lasting bulb
Only the two lasting-bulb rates, since shares do not matter
Only each factory's share, since all bulbs last about equally long
Just the larger factory's rate, since the other is rarely met

items.explain: The example uses how much of the market each factory supplies together with how often each factory's bulbs last.

items.prompt: A parcel can arrive late through a storm, a strike or a breakdown, three separate events. Why is the law of total probability suited to finding the overall chance of a late parcel?

options.label: It picks the single likeliest cause and ignores the others
It assumes the three causes are exactly equally likely
It reverses a chance from one direction to the other
It covers an outcome that can happen through several distinct events

items.explain: The law gives the total probability of an outcome that can be realized through several distinct events, hence its name.

items.prompt: The law of total probability is described as a fundamental rule. Which two kinds of probability does it connect?

options.label: Chances before and chances after a coin has been flipped
Marginal probabilities and conditional probabilities
Chances for single events and chances for infinite series
Theoretical chances and chances found by experiment

items.explain: It relates marginal probabilities to conditional probabilities.

items.prompt: The law of alternatives is called a special case of the law of total probability. To which kind of random variables does it apply?

options.label: Discrete random variables
Only variables with no possible outcomes
Variables that always give the same outcome
Only variables measured in whole hours

items.explain: The law of alternatives is the special case for discrete random variables.

items.prompt: A writer refers to the 'overall probability' of an outcome in an informal piece. Which result is most likely meant?

options.label: The chance of the outcome within one chosen subgroup only
The chance of the outcome once the first event is known
The total chance, as found by the law of total probability
The chance that no event in the list will occur

items.explain: The result of the law of total probability is sometimes called average probability, or overall probability in less formal writings.

paragraphs.heading: One outcome, several routes
paragraphs.text: The law of total probability is a basic rule of probability theory. It links marginal probabilities, meaning overall chances, to conditional probabilities. It works out the total chance of an outcome that can come about through several separate events. That is where the name comes from: it adds up the routes to get the whole.

paragraphs.heading: An average with weights
paragraphs.text: The rule takes the form of a sum, with one term for each separate event. That sum can be read as a weighted average, so the overall chance of the outcome, P (A), is sometimes called its "average probability". In less formal writing it is also called the "overall probability". If one of the events has probability zero, its term is simply left out of the sum, since P (A ∣ Bₙ) is finite.

paragraphs.heading: Two light bulb factories
paragraphs.text: Here is an everyday case. Two factories, X and Y, supply light bulbs to the market. Factory X makes 60% of the bulbs on sale and factory Y makes the other 40%. Bulbs from X last more than 5000 hours in 99% of cases, while bulbs from Y do so in 95% of cases. So, for example, P (A ∣ B_Y) = 95/100 is the chance that a bulb from Y lasts over 5000 hours. If you buy a bulb without knowing where it came from, what is the chance it lasts longer than 5000 hours?

paragraphs.heading: Putting it together
paragraphs.text: The answer weights each factory's success rate by its share of the market. The 99% rate counts for the 60% of bulbs that come from X, and the 95% rate counts for the 40% from Y. Adding these weighted parts gives the answer: each bulb you buy has a 97.4% chance of working for more than 5000 hours.

paragraphs.heading: Other names for the rule
paragraphs.text: The same idea turns up under several names. Some people use the name for the law of alternatives, a special case that covers discrete random variables. One author calls it the "Rule of Average Conditional Probabilities", and another speaks of the "continuous law of alternatives" for the continuous case. Grimmett and Welsh call it the partition theorem, a name they also give to a related rule, the law of total expectation.
